newsitem.title: USA: U.S. faults Cyprus for buying Russian missiles.
newsitem.headline: U.S. faults Cyprus for buying Russian missiles.

text.p: The United States on Monday sharply criticised Cyprus for agreeing to purchase Russian anti-aircraft missiles, which it said would introduce a new and destabilising element on the island and undermine peace efforts.

"The United States regrets this step and we have made it clear to the government of Cyprus and others that we believe that this will complicate efforts to achieve a lasting peace in Cyprus," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"The (Greek) Cypriot decision introduces a new and destablizing element on this island and in the region at the very time that the international community is exploring ways to foster political cooperation to significantly advance a (peace) settlement," he said.
In addition to expressing its "great displeasure" to Cyprus over the sale, the United States also communicated its "great disappointment" to Russia, Burns added.

The planned acquisition from Russia of the S-300 system, with a 90-mile (145 km) range, is the first step by the Cypriot government toward building a credible air defence system. Diplomats said the missiles would neutralise the air superiority Turkey has had in the region since 1974, when its troops invaded the northern third of Cyprus in response to a short-lived coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
"Cyprus is already one of the most militarized regions in the world. Turkey maintains a very large military force on the island and both sides are already heavily armed," Burns told reporters.

"Lasting security and peace for the people of Cyprus can only be achieved at the bargaining table with all sides committed to finding a solution. The past has shown that importing weapons has brought only arms increase from the other sides. This new missile system threatsn to take the arms buildup on Cyprus to a new and disturbing qualitative level," he said.
Regardless of when this system is deployed, he said, "we believe that the conclusion of this sales contract makes any mediation effort that much more difficult and it harms the political atmosphere."

President Bill Clinton remains determined to work with the international community on a peace settlement for Cyprus but the two sides -- and their partners in the region including Greece and Turkey -- "must also be prepared to make the tough choices necessary in negotiations," Burns said. This includes reducing defence expenditures, ending provocative military exercises and improving safety along the Cyprus ceasefire line, he said.
The missile deal was concluded last weekend but it was unclear when the air defence system would be put into place.

The agreement has raised concern in Turkey, where Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said Greek Cypriot authorities were not working for peace. United Nations' resolutions on the island have repeatedly called on both sides to cut their military spending.
International efforts to reunite the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, split by a U.N.-patrolled ceasefire line since Turkey's 1974 invasion, under a federal system have gathered pace recently.

One reason is Cyprus's desire to join the European Union. Accession talks are scheduled to start next year but the EU would like to see first a solution to the island's division, a source of tension between NATO allies Turkey and Greece.

Greece and Cyprus have a joint defence pact -- as do Turkey and the Turkish Cypriot administration in the island's north. The missiles will be deployed to protect an air and navy base under construction on the island's western coast.

The bases, part of the defence pact with Greece, should be completed this year. The system is also expected to protect an air corridor between Cyprus and Greece, whose combat aircraft would intervene in the event of renewed hostilities on the island. Cyprus is only a few minutes away for combat aircraft taking off from the Turkish mainland.
